title: Catch the Perseid Meteor Shower: Nature's Fireworks Show!
summary:
Have you ever seen a shooting star? They're actually tiny bits of dust and rock from comets that burn up in our sky. This week, you might see dozens of them! The Perseid meteor shower is peaking on the night of August 12 into August 13, 2026. That's when you could see between 50 and 100 meteors every hour. That's like a firework show made by nature!

This year is extra special because there's a new moon, which means the sky will be extra dark. That makes the meteors easier to spot. The Perseids are named after the constellation Perseus because they seem to come from there. But really, they come from a comet called Swift-Tuttle. This comet is huge—about 16 miles wide! It orbits the Sun every 133 years. It last came by in 1992, and it'll be back in 2126.

You can see the meteors from both hemispheres, but the best views are in the Northern Hemisphere. To watch, find a dark, open space away from city lights. You don't need a telescope—just your eyes! Give your eyes about 15 minutes to adjust to the dark. Then look up and wait. Be patient, and you'll see streaks of light zoom across the sky. Some are even as bright as Jupiter or Venus—those are called fireballs.

So grab a blanket, lie down, and enjoy the show. And don't forget to make a wish when you see a shooting star. It might just come true!
why_it_matters: You don't need special equipment, so this is a rare free chance to see space acting like a natural firework show from your own backyard.

Earth passes through the dusty trail of Comet Swift-Tuttle every August, which is why the Perseids show up at about the same time each year.
Meteor showers are best seen from dark, open places because city lights can make the streaks hard to notice.
